subject: religious-studies
title: The Garden of Theodicy
welcome_lead: Walk through the garden where Augustine and Irenaeus tend the difficult plant called theodicy.
meta_desc: A-Level Religious Studies adventure on the problem of evil and major theodicies.
final_note: Theodicy is not a tidy proof but a way of holding faith and suffering together.

concepts.def: An attempt to justify the goodness of God in the face of the existence of evil; the term was coined by Leibniz in 1710.
Mackie's formulation of the problem: God's omnipotence, omnibenevolence, and the existence of evil cannot all be true together.
The view that evil is a privation of good (privatio boni), entering creation through the free-will Fall of angels and humans.
The view that humans are created immature and grow through suffering into the likeness of God; developed by John Hick as 'soul-making'.
Plantinga's argument that a world with free creatures who sometimes choose evil is more valuable than a world of determined goodness.
The ancient challenge: if God is willing but unable, He is impotent; if able but unwilling, malevolent; if both, why is there evil?

walkthroughs.body_html:
In Confessions and City of God, Augustine (354-430) argued that God created a perfect world and evil is not a substance but a privation (privatio boni), a falling away from goodness.

Moral evil entered through the misuse of free will by angels and by Adam and Eve; natural evil is a consequence of this cosmic Fall. We are 'seminally present' in Adam and so share in guilt and punishment.

John Hick's Evil and the God of Love (1966) develops Irenaeus' two-stage creation. Humans are made in the image of God but must grow into His likeness through moral and spiritual development.

An 'epistemic distance' from God is necessary for genuine freedom, and a world containing real challenges is required for virtues like courage and compassion to be cultivated.

Alvin Plantinga, in God, Freedom, and Evil (1974), argues that it is logically possible that every possible free creature suffers from 'transworld depravity', so even an omnipotent God cannot create a world of free beings who always choose good.

This shifts the debate from a logical problem of evil to an evidential one, which Plantinga regards as much weaker.
